meta.title: Two Questions That Sound Alike
meta.summary: Chord-scale theory and this pathway's modes use the same seven names for two different questions, and a three-line test tells you which one you're actually answering.

spans.text: . That's the shape this question takes once you're actually playing — one mode name reaching for each chord in a moving progression, drawn from all seven names this pathway has spent five chapters teaching. You'll meet it everywhere once you go looking: real charts, backing tracks, other guitarists talking through a tune.

Take it seriously before pulling it apart, because it's a real practice with a real job. A chord that's on its way somewhere else still has notes available over it in the moment it's sounding, and chord-scale theory is the name for labelling them, one chord at a time. It borrows this pathway's mode names because the note sets genuinely are the same — D Dorian and C major share every note there is.

Here's exactly what's different, in this pathway's own terms. A mode, the way this pathway uses the word, is a claim about home: a note set, plus a tonic asserted from outside the scale, plus a home solid enough to be worth asserting —
When the Progression Starts to Function

just showed the Key Detector agreeing without a second thought. So "D Dorian over the Dm" isn't a claim that the music is in D Dorian. It's a label for the notes available over one chord, inside a key something else entirely is naming. The mode is doing no work there as a home — none at all.

And here's the blunt version, because it's the whole point of this pathway: a note set with no home isn't a mode. Calling both things "Dorian" is exactly what makes modes feel confusing for years — one use of the word names a home, the other labels a scrap of scale over a chord that's about to move on, and nothing in the syllables tells you which one you're hearing. Neither version of the word is wrong; they're just answering two different questions. Chord-scale theory is a real skill and a genuine topic — it's just not this one. It assumes chords that keep moving, where a mode needs a home that holds still.

items.text: Is something holding one home still, rather than moving through several?
Is that home a chord you can stand on?
Which single note are you leaning on against it?

spans.text: Answer yes to the first two and the third has an answer — you're playing a mode. Answer no to the first, and you're playing in a key, and the mode names hovering over each chord are labels, not homes.
Here's the accounting, mode by mode — the same seven home chords this pathway has been building since chapter 2, and whether each one is a home a scale can actually hold onto.
Only one row says no, and by now you know exactly why — no perfect fifth over
, nothing to stand on, so a vamp built on it hands the tonic to some other note before it ever gets the chance to be Locrian.
Locrian, and the Home That Won't Hold

Five chapters in, and that's the whole test, plus every home chord in one place. What's left is playing: taking each vamp you already know, finding the characteristic note inside a window your hands have held since long before this pathway, and leaning on it until it's unmistakable. Chapter 6 is where that happens.
